summary: Wild chervil is a member of the carrot family up to 3½ feet tall, with fern-like leaves and airy, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers. When it blooms in masses along roadsides and in fields, little else is visible. It spreads quickly by underground stems and lots of seed (800 to 10,000 seeds per plant), and its deep taproot helps it form smothering stands that crowd out native plants and lower plant diversity.
history: Wild chervil is native to Europe and Asia. It colonizes stream corridors, disturbed woods, fields and roadsides.
seasons: It is a spring-blooming perennial: its white flower clusters appear in late spring, then turn into small, dry, long fruits. Most seeds fall close to the parent plant and last in the soil for only one winter.

handling.text: Young plants can be pulled or dug up, but the taproot must come out or the plant can resprout. Cutting it when it flowers can reduce its spread, but this must be finished before the fruits form, because mowing is one of the main ways it spreads.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
